title: Plan mode
description: The agent builds a plan first and waits for your “OK”: “think” kept apart from “do.”

steps.question: You ask an agent: “go through my email and delete the junk.” What does a good agent do first?
steps.answer: It doesn't delete a single message. It shows a plan first — what exactly it thinks is junk — and waits for your “OK.” That is Plan mode.

steps.text: Plan mode means the agent first writes out a plan: the steps it intends to take. Only then does it carry them out.

steps.imagePrompt: A small robot holds up a clipboard with a checklist to a person and waits with a pause sign, before starting to sort a messy pile of envelopes.
steps.caption: First the plan and your “OK,” then the work

steps.definition: A lock between “think” and “do”: until you approve the plan, tools are switched off and the agent touches nothing.
steps.example: The plan is ready → you tap “Approve” → only now does the agent start carrying it out.

steps.text: The plan is shown to you for confirmation, so you can correct course before anything is done. If you change it, the agent rebuilds the plan.

steps.caption: Tap a step to cross it out, then tap “Approve.” The number of emails is just an example

steps.text: The point is simple: we keep “think” apart from “do,” and on complex tasks that sharply cuts the number of mistakes. And notice that Plan mode isn't insurance against a silly model. It is insurance against the cost of a mistake. When actions touch real things — files, money, emails — confirming the plan is cheaper than cleaning up afterwards.

steps.instruction: Put the course of Plan mode in order:
items: The agent carries out the steps
The agent hands over the result
steps.explain: Task → plan → your “OK” → work → result. Before the “OK,” no actions.

steps.situation: Two tasks: “rename a hundred files in my project” and “how many days until New Year?”
steps.q: Where is Plan mode really needed?
options: With the files: a mistake is costly, so fix course before acting
With the date: counting days is a hard multi-step task
In both: a plan never hurts
steps.explain: Plan mode is insurance against the cost of a mistake. A simple question doesn't need a gate. It's just an extra tap.

steps.text: Practice. Plan mode is right here in the app, but only for agents you build yourself. Take your own agent or build a new one (Agents → Create agent). A chat with the Builder opens: it asks a few questions with tick boxes and ends on a “Review your agent” screen. Tick Plan in the Modes section there (or just tell the Builder you want it), then publish the agent. In a chat with that agent, choose Plan and give it a multi-part task. A plan card arrives, and no tool is touched until you tap “Approve.” Try “Request changes” too and see how the plan is rebuilt.

Under the hood, Plan mode now runs on a structured plan engine: a plan is not just text but a list of steps with statuses and a check. The plan card right in the chat lets you approve it, pause it, resume it or cancel it. What that changes is covered in a separate lesson, Structured plans.
In short. Plan mode: plan first → your “OK” → only then actions. The gate keeps tools switched off until you approve. Use it where a mistake is costly, and correct course before anything is done.

options: Builds a plan first, then carries it out
Does everything at once, with no plan or questions
Cancels the task if it is complex
questions.explain: Plan mode separates planning from doing.

questions.q: What does the agent do before the plan is approved?
options: Carries out nothing and touches no tools
It has already done it all and just awaits praise
Carries out only the safe steps
questions.explain: The gate: before your “OK,” no actions.

questions.q: Why show the plan before the work, not after?
options: Fixing course is cheaper before acting than cleaning up after
So the user can see the agent isn't being lazy
It makes the agent finish the task faster
questions.explain: The gate exists because of the cost of a mistake: editing a plan is free, undoing actions is not.
